Near Dark.description:
1987 — USA — Kathryn Bigelow — 94 min — Cert 18

A young man becomes a member of a scavenging vampire ‘family’, in Kathryn Bigelow’s hugely entertaining genre mash-up of horror and western tropes.

Caleb, a cowboy in rural Oklahoma, falls for a mysterious drifter, only to discover she is a member of a roaming ‘family’ of vampires. Seamlessly blending western, noir and road movie tropes with teen romance and a strong gothic tinge, Near Dark established Bigelow as a skilful manipulator of genres and a storyteller attuned to moral ambiguity. An instant cult classic, the nocturnal scenes, popping with cool neon lights, play out to a pulsating Tangerine Dream soundtrack that, like the film, is moody, elegiac and thrillingly tense.

New Writings: 100 Bible Films.description:
Tracing this often-controversial history over 125 years, Matt Page explores silent passion plays and the golden age of the epic, as well more innovative and controversial later biblical films.

Filmmakers have long found adapting the Bible irresistible, from Alice Guy in 1906, via Rossellini, Godard, Buñuel and Scorsese, through to the modern day. Whether it’s a Marxist masterpiece by Pasolini or one of the faith-based adaptations emerging from the US under Trump 2.0, the results have often proved controversial, with their handling of race, religion, sex and politics attracting rancour. Matt Page traces this colourful history over 125 years and five continents asking, what have Biblical films ever done for us? Tickets £6.50.

New Writings: Acting and Performance in.description:
The author of Acting and Performance in Hitchcock argues that, contrary to popular opinion, the director’s films show a fascination with acting.

Although Alfred Hitchcock was notoriously dismissive of actors, this new edited collection argues that acting played a key element of his work. Films discussed include Notorious, Stage Fright and Strangers on a Train. The book provides detailed analysis of some exceptional performances by major stars – from Ivor Novello to Tippi Hedren – and considers performance as a theme across Hitchcock’s oeuvre. Tickets £6.50. See a Big Screen Classics screening of The Birds .

New Writings: Action Heroines in the 21s.description:
‘Action Heroines in the 21st Century’ highlights the changing representation of female protagonists in recent action-led genres.

The new millennium has seen a growing number of films and television series featuring women acting collectively to resist violence and assert agency, reflecting an increasing global foregrounding and rejection of violence towards women. Co-editors Fran Pheasant-Kelly and Christa van Raalte will be joined by several of the book’s contributors to discuss their approaches to women-centred action narratives, from remakes of Charlie’s Angels through to the Western, action-comedies and Marvel’s female superheroes. Tickets £6.50.

_additional_info.title: Action Heroines in the 21st Century – Sisters in Arms

New Writings: Blur by Martine Beugnet.description:
Martine Beugnet discusses film blur not as a technical error but as an essential feature of cinema.

In cinema, when blurriness appears it is either considered an error or a background effect. Martine Beugnet, Professor in Visual Studies at the Université Paris Cité, argues it is an essential feature of the cinema. Blur is the third instalment in the Cutaways series of pocket volumes, which journey through the history of cinema via a single motif or formal device. Tickets £6.50

New Writings: Moving Image \u2013 A User.description:
Two-thirds of the world’s internet traffic is video. The Moving Image is the first definitive manual to help writers, educators and publishers use video more effectively.

In the United States and United Kingdom, people get their news and information more often from screens and speakers than through any other means. Peter B. Kaufman, Associate Director of Development at MIT Open Learning, explains how it’s the moving image – not social media or artificial intelligence – that brings personalities like Trump and Putin to dominate the world stage. Tickets £6.50.

New Writings: Shoah (BFI Classics) with.description:
To celebrate the new edition of the BFI Classic ‘Shoah’, author Sue Vice considers Claude Lanzmann’s work as an influence on films that witness genocide and the Holocaust.

At this launch for the new edition of the BFI Modern Classics volume on Claude Lanzmann’s Shoah (1985) author Sue Vice is joined by film scholars Barry Langford and Libby Saxton to discuss new approaches to this landmark Holocaust documentary. These include the newly available archive of outtakes from the film and its influence over more recent cinematic works about genocide. Tickets £6.50.

On the Margins.description:
We observe the sensationalising of vulnerable groups in multicultural communities.

BBC 1993. Series Producer Charles Bruce. 28min. Digital BBC 1998. Series Editor Mike Finlanson. 29min. Digital Channel 4 1997. Director Lynn Keane. 26min. Digital Britain’s cities became increasingly global communities, which widened the notion of multicultural beyond the traditions of Black and Asian migration. At the same time, tabloid culture crept into multicultural programming, with increasingly sensationalised portrayals of communities. These sensational stories capture how television came to delegitimise those in need of assistance – a predatory tone that has become increasingly prevalent just starting to seep into early 2000s programming.

Open Door.description:
When Community Access television reached Britain’s shores it became an outlet for campaigners who would help to establish multicultural representation on TV.

BBC 1973. BBC Community Programme Unit. 56min. Digital BBC 1979. BBC Community Programme Unit. 30min. Digital Movements which campaigned against mistreatment by the state flourished across Black and Asian communities. In these episodes of Open Door, teachers hold the educational establishment to account, while Southall campaigners respond to the actions taken by police to protect the National Front against mass action protests.

A Pale View of Hills.description:
2025 — Japan — Kei Ishikawa — 123 min

A sterling adaptation of Nobel Prize winner Kazuo Ishiguro’s debut novel, which unfolds in the shadow of Nagasaki.

In this adaptation of Nobel Prize-winning novelist Kazuo Ishiguro’s striking debut, a woman confronts uncomfortable memories of Nagasaki during the Second World War. Desperate to understand her family’s history in Japan before her birth, Niki questions her mother Etsuko about her life in Nagasaki, subsequent move to England and its impact upon her loved ones. Spanning two timelines and lightly excavating the author’s own family history and cultural heritage, this poignant tale of loss and exile under the shadow of the atom bomb is a moving, and ultimately hopeful, account of the generational impact of war. Aiko’s sensitive, compelling portrayal of Nikki guides us from the present to the past, while Ishikawa’s script and direction subtly capture the nuances of Ishiguro’s 1982 novel, skilfully guiding us through Japan’s tumultuous recent history. Jason Wood, BFI Executive Director of Public Programme and Audiences Contains scenes of animal slaughter.

The Passing of the Third Floor Back + in.description:
1935 — UK — Berthold Viertel — 91 min

A mysterious stranger arrives at an English boarding house and transforms the lives of its residents.

One of the most accomplished British films of the 1930s, this fantasy melodrama boasts a wonderful ensemble cast headed by one of the industry’s finest imports: Conrad Veidt. Set in that most evocative, claustrophobic locale, the English boarding house, Jerome K. Jerome’s play brings together characters from different classes to play out its drama of sexual and class politics, reflecting on relationships and generational shift. The script was co-written by Alma Reville (Alfred Hitchcock’s wife and early collaborator), whose sensitive depiction of female characters is one of the film’s greatest assets, particularly Rène Ray as the put-upon maid and Beatrix Lehmann as a bitter spinster.

_additional_info.title: The Passing of the Third Floor Back

Planet of the Apes.description:
1968 — USA — Franklin J. Schaffner — 112 min

An astronaut lands in a world where apes rule over humanity, in this 1960s sci-fi parable.

Heston’s astronaut crash-lands on a seemingly barren planet and is captured by simian soldiers. It’s a topsy-turvy world where apes rule and humans are their mute subjects. Both an accessible fantasy and a chilling parable, Planet of the Apes has influenced countless films over the decades, becoming a sci-fi classic.

Point Break.description:
1991 — USA — Kathryn Bigelow — 122 min — Cert 15

Keanu Reeves and Patrick Swayze star as an undercover agent and a charismatic surfer in Kathryn Bigelow’s classic action hit.

FBI agent Johnny Utah goes undercover to infiltrate a gang of Californian surfers suspected of committing bank robberies. He finds inspiration, and channels more than a little adrenaline, when he encounters Bodhi, the group’s leader – a free spirit with a penchant for extreme sports. With tight framing and kinetic handheld camera work, Bigelow plunges the audience into the heart of the conflict, while playing with genre expectations and representations of masculinity, to deliver a top-notch, white-knuckle actioner. See the Relaxed screening of Point Break .

Relaxed screening: Point Break + intro a.description:
1991 — USA — Kathryn Bigelow — 122 min — Cert 15

Keanu Reeves and Patrick Swayze star as an undercover agent and a charismatic surfer in Kathryn Bigelow’s classic action hit.

FBI agent Johnny Utah goes undercover to investigate a gang of surfers who are suspected of being behind a string of bank robberies. As he gets closer to cracking the case, an unlikely friendship with the gang’s charismatic spiritual leader threatens to tip his world into chaos. Kathryn Bigelow’s supremely entertaining film is one of the great Hollywood action thrillers. The film will be introduced by neurodivergent film programmer Issy Macleod. There will be a post-screening discussion where we will explore the film from neurodiverse perspectives In partnership with Stims Collective. Relaxed screenings are presented each month for those in the neuro-diverse community and their assistants and carers. More detailed information can be found at bfi.org.uk/relaxed . Tickets £4. See other screenings of Point Break .

Portrait of a Lady on Fire.description:
2019 — France — Céline Sciamma — 122 min — Cert 15

Céline Sciamma’s widely celebrated tale of love and yearning between two young women in 18th-century France.

Artist Marianne arrives at a solitary house outside a gloomy coastal town in 18th-century France. She’s tasked with covertly painting the estate’s heir, Héloïse, an aloof young bride-to-be. But between stolen glances and secrets spilled, a romance unfurls, challenging what is true and what is seen to be right. Masterfully shot and decisively feminist, Sciamma’s sublime drama is one of the most evocative depictions of desire and longing to hit the screen. Contains themes of abortion. Also available on BFI Player

_additional_info.title: Portrait of a Lady on Fire

Opening Night: Primavera + intro and Q&A.description:
2025 — Italy-France — Damiano Michieletto — 110 min

Cinema Made in Italy opens with this enthralling period drama inspired by the life of composer Antonio Vivaldi.

This authentic, beautifully realised musical drama is set in an 18th century Italian church that doubles as an orphanage for young women who perform in its orchestra. Drawing on the real life of Vivaldi, Primavera details the consequences that ensue when Cecilia, a talented protégé of the legendary composer (played by the wonderful Tecla Insolia) rebels against the orphanage’s draconian strictures. Italy 1991. Director Bruno Bozzetto. 9min. Digital. With English subtitles In the natural course of earth’s evolution, five or a thousand years represent just a handful of seconds. What is the role of mankind on this boundless stage?

The Promised Land + Q&A with actor Danie.description:
1974 — Poland — Andrzej Wajda — 163 min — Cert 15

Andrzej Wajda was nominated for an Academy Award for this satire about wealth, capitalism and industrialisation.

During the Industrial Revolution, three friends decide to open a textile factory to make their fortune. But friendships, personal relationships and moral values are soon tested. An adaptation of Nobel Prize-winning author Stanisław Reymont’s novel, Wajda’s film is a compelling and continually pertinent indictment of rampant capitalism and humanity’s more selfish impulses. Wajda’s first Academy Award-nominated drama remains one of his most celebrated films. See other screenings of The Promised Land .

Reece Shearsmith Presents: Psycho II + i.description:
1983 — USA — Richard Franklin — 112 min — Cert 15

22 years later, Norman Bates is released and returns home only to be thrown in the middle of a new series of murders.

Despite protests from the family of Marion Crane, who was killed in the Bates Motel some two decades before, her murderer Norman Bates is released from custody and returns to the old family home. With voices haunting him and several new unsolved murders, Bates is forced to confront some home truths. Though rarely screened since its release, Psycho II is an impressive follow up to Hitchcock’s 1960 classic and provided Perkins with another opportunity to shine in the role that he will always be associated with.

Re-connecting the Diaspora.description:
Multicultural TV served as a point of reconnection between Black and Asian Britons and their nations of origin.

BBC 1983. Series Producer Keith Sheather. 30min. Digital Channel 4 1987. Director Peter Emina. 40min. Digital Channel 4 1988. Director Christopher Spencer. 52min. Digital Dreams of returning punctuated many migrant experiences and TV served to foster connections to stories back home, offering depictions of the realities for returners. They offered depictions of the realities of returners. These documentaries kept people in the diaspora up to date on the social climate of their home nations, even focusing on holding to account scam artists who were trying to extort those attempting to navigate returning home.

Reflecting on Stuart Hall\u2019s Impact.description:
We look back on the impact of Professor Stuart Hall with this screening and discussion, in collaboration with the Stuart Hall Foundation.

BBC 1979. BBC Community Programme Unit in association with Campaign Against Racism in the Media. 29min. Digital UK 1985. Director Yugesh Walia. 39min. Digital Professor Stuart Hall, founder of British cultural studies, was a leading thinker whose ideas on diaspora, Marxism, race and class transformed how British society is understood. His pioneering work on media, remains essential for analysing the political and cultural dynamics of multiculturalism. We look back on his impact in association with the Stuart Hall Foundation, through a screening and discussion featuring programmes he made with CARM (Campaign Against Racism in the Media) and the Commission for Racial Equality. Tickets £6.50.

_additional_info.title: Reflecting on Stuart Hall’s Impact in association with the Stuart Hall Foundation

Representation of Women on Multicultural.description:
Across multicultural television there were layered and, at times, insufficient portrayals of the lives of women.

BBC 1987. Asian Unit Presentation. 25min. Digital. With English subtitles Channel 4 1996. Director Rakha Singh. 26min. Digital BBC 2000. Director Geeta Gupta. 29min. Digital Programmes focusing on the lives of Asian Women initially looked at the domestic sphere, before more serious investigations centred on domestic violence and self-harm. Despite Black women having prominent roles in production and presenting across multicultural shows, there was relatively little coverage of issues affecting Black women. This 1996 episode of Black Bag is a rare exception.

_additional_info.title: Representation of Women on Multicultural TV

Preview: Resurrection.description:
2025 — China-France-USA — Bi Gan — 156 min — Cert 15

Bi Gan’s epic sci-fi drama is an ambitious ode to the beauty and power of cinema.

In a version of the future where humanity has sacrificed the ability to dream, one lonesome creature secretly retains the power to experience them, until a curious woman uncovers his inner worlds. Traversing the breadth of cinematic styles across six chapters, Bi Gan’s sprawling odyssey is a masterful tribute to film history and its ability to shape us as human beings. Contains scenes of graphic violence and flashing images.

The Revolution Was Televised.description:
Successive uprisings across Britain responded to a climate of hostile policing. We review these actions through the lens of multicultural reporting.

LWT 1980. LWT. Director Trevor Hampton. 26min. Digital LWT 1981. LWT. 5min. Digital LWT 1982. Director David Coulter. 28min. Digital BBC 1984. Series Producer Christopher Graham. 30min. Digital LWT 1985. Editor Mike Townson. 15min. Digital Skin’s non-fiction output was prescient. In 1980, it covered the issue of aggressive behaviour by the police towards Black communities, presaging the uprisings in cities across the UK – from Toxteth and Handsworth to Brixton, Chapeltown and Moss Side – which saw young Black people rejecting the brutal climate of policing. During these events, multicultural investigative programming was shunted off air. It was only able to reflect critically on these events in the years that followed.

Rough Treatment + intro by film critic a.description:
1978 — Poland — Andrzej Wajda — 130 min — Cert 15

Andrzej Wajda’s powerful drama is a deeply affecting portrait of a man who unexpectedly loses everything.

The professional and personal lives of a respected journalist unravel unexpectedly, forcing him to reflect on his life to date. But will he be able to turn his life around? Co-written with Agnieszka Holland, Wajda’s drama is an affecting portrait of a man navigating an oppressive political system and a labyrinth of complicated human relations. See other screenings of Rough Treatment .

The Secret Agent.description:
2025 — Brazil-France-Germany-Netherlands — Kleber Mendonça Filho — 158 min

Kleber Mendonça Filho delivers a stinging portrait of life for an academic on the run in 1970s dictator-ruled Brazil.

Kleber Mendonça Filho navigates Brazil’s painful past to paint a loving portrayal of a place and its people, in this slow burning and hugely entertaining political thriller. It’s Carnival week, 1977, in dictatorship-ruled Brazil. Marcelo, a widower on the run arrives in Recife, hoping to reunite with his young son and flee the country. He finds refuge in a resistance commune run by a charismatic 70-year-old woman, but chaos soon catches up with him. Corrupt forces from his previous life are on his tail and he faces further duplicity in the city – his escape trickier with each turn. Combining political statement with light-hearted sentiment, Bacurau and Aquarius writer-director Kleber Mendonça Filho’s novelistic feature revels in playful genre-bending detours – including a gleefully deranged B-movie inspired sequence – and soulful emotions to deliver a sweaty, sun-drenched and masterfully acted ride that is always grounded in love: for Brazil and for cinema. Diana Cipriano, Programme & Research Coordinator Contains scenes of graphic violence. Audio Description available at all screenings. Seniors\u2019 Free Matinee: Mandabi + in.description:
1968 — Senegal-France — Ousmane Sembène — 92 min

Ousmane Sembène’s revered film served as a major inspiration for Akinola Davies Jr., director of My Father’s Shadow.

Ibrahima Dieng lives with his two wives and seven children in Dakar. Unemployed, his fortunes change when his nephew sends him a significant money order from Paris. But greed and corruption soon unravel his simple family life. One of the masterpieces of African cinema, Mandabi is an astute exploration of postcolonial identity, capitalism and the complexity of the human ego. Free for the over-60s (booking by phone or in person only), otherwise normal matinee price.

Sir\u00e2t.description:
2025 — Spain-France — Óliver Laxe — 115 min — Cert 15

A father looking for his daughter joins a community of hedonistic travellers on a journey that will change all their lives, in Óliver Laxe’s existential speculative thriller.

Exploring themes of endurance, surrender and inner stillness, Óliver Laxe’s striking, wholly original existential thriller is a richly sensory encounter that lingers long after viewing. A father, with his son in tow, searches the Moroccan desert for his daughter, who absconded from home and might have taken up with a group of revellers seeking an alternative way of living. What starts out as a remarkable, other-worldly journey, transforms into a meditative inquiry into loss, grief and spirituality. Central to the film is its evocative score – a powerhouse of churning, grinding techno by composer Kanding Ray. More than an accompaniment, the music operates as an emotional, spatial and temporal modulator – one that invites us to abandon interpretation and submit to Laxe’s and utterly unique perspective on the world. A visually and aurally arresting road trip, which demands to be seen on the biggest screen, Sirât is a profound work by one of contemporary cinema’s most distinctive and poetic voices. Stuart Brown, Director of Programme and Distribution See screenings of Sirât at BFI IMAX . See our Sirât Member Salon .

A father looking for his daughter joins a community of hedonistic travellers on a journey that will change all their lives, in Óliver Laxe’s existential speculative thriller.

Exploring themes of endurance, surrender and inner stillness, Óliver Laxe’s striking, wholly original existential thriller is a richly sensory encounter that lingers long after viewing. A father, with his son in tow, searches the Moroccan desert for his daughter, who absconded from home and might have taken up with a group of revellers seeking an alternative way of living. What starts out as a remarkable, other-worldly journey, transforms into a meditative inquiry into loss, grief and spirituality. Central to the film is its evocative score – a powerhouse of churning, grinding techno by composer Kanding Ray. More than an accompaniment, the music operates as an emotional, spatial and temporal modulator – one that invites us to abandon interpretation and submit to Laxe’s and utterly unique perspective on the world. A visually and aurally arresting road trip, which demands to be seen on the biggest screen, Sirât is a profound work by one of contemporary cinema’s most distinctive and poetic voices. Stuart Brown, Director of Programme and Distribution Members can book an advanced joint ticket to this screening and the Sirât Member Salon for themselves and their guests in advance. Members who watch the film on another date are welcome to attend the free Salon discussion and show their Membership Card for admission, on a first come first served basis. See other screenings of Sirât .

Family Funday Preview: Stitch Head + Q&A.description:
2025 — Germany-Luxembourg-UK — Steve Hudson — 92 min

Guy Bass’s acclaimed 2011 graphic novel reaches the screen in resplendent and thrilling form with this beautifully crafted animation.

In a castle laboratory high above a little town, a mad professor obsesses over his monster experiments. As each new creature emerges, older ones are cast aside and left feeling ignored. Stitch Head, the first of the scientist’s abandoned experiments, decides to join a circus, unaware of how untrustworthy its ringmaster is and that his friends in the castle are now in danger. Tickets for under 16s £4. Otherwise standard ticket price (Members pay £2.50 less). Sunday 8 February 10:45 BFI Southbank Foyer Total running time 60min Come to the main foyer and meet Pete Williamson, the ilustrator of the Stitch Head books, who will give a drawing masterclass. There are also opportunities to make your own short, animated stories alongside our usual arts and crafts station. Free to ticket holders of the Funday screening.

Strange Days.description:
1995 — USA — Kathryn Bigelow — 145 min — Cert 18

Ralph Fiennes’ ex-cop is enmeshed in a conspiracy that threatens to tear Los Angeles apart, in Kathryn Bigelow’s dystopian thriller.

In a dystopian LA of the (then) future, street hustler Nero illegally sells VR-like recordings that allow users to experience the memories of others. A shocking recording, which could bring the city to its knees, falls into his hands, drawing him and his long-suffering friend into a dangerous conspiracy. Bigelow’s sci-fi neo-noir features spectacularly staged sequences, alongside themes of addiction, voyeurism and abuses of power that drive this top-notch, state of the nation thriller. Contains scenes of racism, sexual violence and police brutality.

The Subnormal Scandal.description:
The scandal of ESN schools had a lasting legacy in British schools. We look at how education was covered in multicultural programming across these years.

BBC 1983. ALTARF in association with BBC Community Programme Unit. 29 min. Digital LWT 1981. Director Trevor Hampton. 26min. Digital BBC 2021. Director Lyttanya Shannon. 60min. Digital The structural inequality of British schooling a recurring topic in multicultural television. Black children in the school system were labelled ‘educationally subnormal’ and forced into specialist, which often under-educated them. Recognition of the scandal of subnormal schools has taken a long time to be recognised. The 2021 BBC documentary was an important landmark in this respect.

Sweetheart + intro and Q&A.description:
2025 — Italy — Margherita Spampinato — 90 min

An unusual and affecting story about a young boy staying with an elderly woman.

A young boy from the hustle and modern bustle of Milan is deposited for the summer with his great aunt in Sicily, whose old-fashioned lifestyle is distinctly at odds with his own. It features a captivating, charismatic performance by veteran actor Aurora Quattrocchi, who deservedly won the Best Actress Award at the Locarno Film Festival.

Three Coins in the Fountain.description:
1954 — USA — Jean Negulesco — 102 min

Revel in Jean Negulesco’s sweeping romance about three American women working in Rome.

At Rome’s Trevi Fountain, three American women discuss their dreams of love and a life in beautiful Italy. Their wishes are granted when romance finds its way to them through the streets of this ancient city, but in ways more complex than they had envisaged. Oscars were awarded to the sumptuous cinematography and music, while the film was nominated for Best Picture.

Closing Night: Three Goodbyes + intro an.description:
2025 — Italy-Spain — Isabel Coixet — 120 min

Cinema Made in Italy closes with this bittersweet, inspiring drama about a couple’s lives following their breakup.

A chef and a schoolteacher suddenly break up, with very different consequences for their futures. Adapted from Michela Murgia’s final, partly autobiographical, novel, Three Goodbyes is a moving account of emotional turmoil and reconciliation. Spanish director Coixet’s (My Life without Me) beautifully made Italian melodrama profits from the excellent central performances of Rohrwacher and Germano.

The Wedding.description:
1972 — Poland — Andrzej Wajda — 103 min — Cert 15

Wajda employs hypnotic music and exciting cinematography to adapt a landmark Polish play.

Stanisław Wyspiański’s influential 1901 play details a marriage ceremony between a poet and peasant. The wedding party is attended by a cross-section of society. However, the veneer of harmony is broken when ghosts – drawn from local history and legend – appear to the revellers. Wajda’s adaptation employs dizzying cinematography and creates an eerie atmosphere as he presents a searing critique of the nation. It became one of the most culturally significant works of Polish cinema. The screening of The Wedding on Wednesday 11 February will be introduced by Professor Ewa Mazierska, University of Lancashire.

The Wedding + intro by Professor Ewa Maz.description:
1972 — Poland — Andrzej Wajda — 103 min — Cert 15

Wajda employs hypnotic music and exciting cinematography to adapt a landmark Polish play.

Stanisław Wyspiański’s influential 1901 play details a marriage ceremony between a poet and peasant. The wedding party is attended by a cross-section of society. Joint ticket available with An Introduction to Andrzej Wajda on Wednesday 11 February 18:20 NFT3, tickets £17, concessions £14 (Members pay £2.50 less). Book in person at the box office or by phone on 020 7928 3232. See other screenings of The Wedding .

The Weight of Water.description:
2000 — USA — Kathryn Bigelow — 113 min — Cert 15

Two stories of family jealousy and hidden passions intersect in Kathryn Bigelow’s rarely screened adaptation of Anita Shreve’s bestseller.

A photojournalist travels to a remote island off the New Hampshire coast to research the murders of Norwegian immigrants in the late 1800s. As she digs deeper into the story, she finds her own life paralleling that of a witness to the crime. In this sumptuous, emotionally resonant and piercingly intelligent adaption of Anita Shreve’s acclaimed novel, Bigelow (whose own mother immigrated to America from Norway) fluidly interweaves parallel stories of jealousy and repressed passions. Please note that the print we are using has French subtitles included, but the film is in English.

Wendy and Lucy + intro by writer and edi.description:
2008 — USA — Kelly Reichardt — 80 min — Cert 15

Kelly Reichardt’s third feature, a deceptively simple tale of a lost dog, is a fascinating study of loneliness and loss.

The aspirations of Williams’ young drifter from Indiana are thwarted when her car grinds to a halt in small-town Oregon and she loses her beloved dog Lucy. This nuanced and profoundly moving study of breakdown and loss also riffs on the road-movie genre and finely observes the economic fallout of corporate America. Michelle Williams is luminous in the first of her collaborations with Reichardt, whose own dog features in the film. See other screenings of Wendy and Lucy .

Wendy and Lucy.description:
2008 — USA — Kelly Reichardt — 80 min — Cert 15

Kelly Reichardt’s third feature, a deceptively simple tale of a lost dog, is a fascinating study of loneliness and loss.

The aspirations of Williams’ young drifter from Indiana are thwarted when her car grinds to a halt in small-town Oregon and she loses her beloved dog Lucy. This nuanced and profoundly moving study of breakdown and loss also riffs on the road-movie genre and finely observes the economic fallout of corporate America. Michelle Williams is luminous in the first of her collaborations with Reichardt, whose own dog features in the film. The screening of Wendy and Lucy on Wednesday 4 March will be introduced by writer and editor Laura Staab.

West Indies: The Fugitive Slaves of Libe.description:
1979 — France-Algeria-Mauritania — Med Hondo — 113 min

Med Hondo’s spectacular musical traces the history of the West Indies.

On paper, Mauritanian director Med Hondo’s film seems difficult to believe: a single-set song-and-dance voyage through four centuries of colonialism, enslavement, liberation struggles and modern immigration – in just 110 minutes. On screen, it’s astonishing to behold the successful realisation of such an ambitious project. One of the greatest movies ever made, Hondo’s thrillingly passionate cri de coeur remains a troubling, resonant work.

_additional_info.title: West Indies: The Fugitive Slaves of Liberty

40th anniversary screening: Working Girl.description:
1986 — USA — Lizzie Borden — 93 min — Cert 18

Lizzie Borden’s landmark independent drama charts a few days in the professional and personal lives of sex workers in a Manhattan brothel.

In New York City, Yale graduate Molly attempts to bankroll her photography business by working at a high-end brothel. Her days are filled with the demands of men and her fellow sex workers, and are punctuated by the monotonous dramas of any workplace environment. Borden’s portrayal of sex work is a radical exploration of life under capitalism, a piercing study of sexual politics and an astute overview of the complexity of women’s lives.

A Year of School + intro and Q&A.description:
2025 — Italy-France — Laura Samani — 90 min

This acutely observed portrait of a teenage girl’s experiences at a new school is an impressive coming-of-age drama by Laura Samani.

Small Body director Laura Samani’s second feature is a sharply observed coming-of-age tale, sympathetically adapted from the novel by Giani Stuparich. A teenage Swedish girl starts a new school in Trieste. Entering an all-male class, she embarks on a rollercoaster ride of emotions and experiences.

A Zed and Two Noughts + intro by Justin.description:
1985 — UK — Peter Greenaway — 117 min — Cert 15

Twin zoologists take extreme steps to feed their obsession with death and decay in animals, in Peter Greenaway’s visually stunning early work.

A pair of twin zoologists, grieving the death of their wives in a collision involving a car and a Swan, gradually form a bond with the woman who was driving the vehicle that caused their loved ones’ demise. The brothers become obsessed with death and decay in animals, creating time-lapse films to further their understanding. Rich in imagery and visually stunning, this early feature by Peter Greenaway is unparalleled in its re-invention and challenge to narrative cinema of this or any time. See other screenings of A Zed and Two Noughts . Also available on BFI Player

A Zed and Two Noughts.description:
